description: Our Mission: For the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge, we are building an interactive, layered spatial dashboard designed specifically for an astronaut's surface EVA (Extravehicular Activity). By integrating NASA’s topographical, thermal, and space weather datasets, we aim to create a hyper localized  navigation interface that helps future crews avoid environmental hazards, track radiation exposure, and map out the most efficient routes for collecting geologic samples.
summary:
When human explorers take their first steps on Mars, they will face an unforgiving vacuum with zero GPS, treacherous terrain drops, and an Earth radio delay of up to 22 minutes. Ground control cannot rescue them in real time.

To solve this life-critical challenge, we developed Mars Sentinel—an autonomous Interplanetary Survival Guide and surface EVA navigation workstation for human Marswalks around Jezero Crater.

Mars Sentinel directly solves the challenge by synthesizing multi-mission NASA data into an integrated, tactical heads-up display. It layers sub-meter MRO HiRISE and CTX orbital imagery with a 20-meter digital elevation model, real-time Perseverance MEDA atmospheric telemetry, and MSL Curiosity RAD radiation tracking. Its safety-first routing engine enforces non-negotiable rules—blocking slopes over 25° and maintaining a 40-meter hazard buffer—while plotting safe traverses to actual Perseverance rock-core caches within an 8-hour life-support ceiling.

Mars Sentinel is vital because it bridges the gap between robotic orbiters and human survival. It gives future crews the local autonomy needed to protect life-support consumables, navigate extreme topography, and conduct transformative science safely on an alien world.
details:
Mars Sentinel

An Interplanetary Survival Guide for Humanity’s First Marswalks

Live App: mars-sentinel.vercel.app

Base: Octavia E. Butler Landing, Jezero Crater

The Problem: Survival on an Unforgiving World

Mars is not just remote; it is lethal. With an atmospheric pressure under 1% of Earth's, nighttime temperatures dropping to −79 °C, zero GPS satellites, unshielded radiation, and up to a 22-minute communication delay to Earth, a basic map is not enough. Astronauts need an Interplanetary Survival Guide.

Mars Sentinel turns decades of robotic NASA data into an autonomous, real-time survival guide for surface spacewalks (EVAs). It translates complex orbital scans into four simple rules of survival: know your terrain, respect your life-support limits, monitor your radiation dose, and always guarantee a safe path back to base.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Mars Sentinel gives astronauts an autonomous navigation co-pilot across a 12 km × 12 km operational grid (20-meter cells) in Jezero Crater:

  • High-Resolution Terrain Engine: Pre-processes USGS/NASA elevation data (JEZ_ctx_B_soc_008_DTM) into lightweight 32-bit binary arrays (elevation.f32, slope.f32) so hazard calculations happen instantly in the browser without lag.
    1. Strict 25° Slope Cutoff: Spacesuits easily lose traction on steep regolith. The system blocks paths through slopes steeper than 25°.
    2. 40-Meter Hazard Buffer: Enforces a mandatory 40-meter standoff distance from cliff edges, loose scree, and unverified ground.
  • Sub-Meter Visuals: Fuses NASA Mars Trek imagery from MRO HiRISE (25 cm/pixel) and CTX (6 m/pixel) so astronauts can clearly identify surface boulders and landmarks.
  • Multi-Scale Views: Seamlessly transitions from the 2D tactical navigation grid to an interactive 3D Mars globe (/globe.html) rendered with real MOLA elevation data.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Protects Spacesuit Consumables: An astronaut's life depends on their Primary Life Support System (PLSS). Mars Sentinel calculates exact uphill climbs and descents (+107 m / −107 m) and total outside time against a strict 8-hour EVA ceiling and 5 km walk-back limit.
  • Safety Explora Sector Scoring: Evaluates all 8 compass directions from the base to show which sectors have the most safe, flat ground (highlighting 9.8 km² of safe ground to the West) and the clearest paths to sample sites.
  • Guides Mission Science: Plots safe routes directly to verified Perseverance rock-core targets (Skinner Ridge, Wildcat Ridge, Observation Mountain, Cheyava Falls), allocating 20 minutes of collection time per stop within the safe return window.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Tools like NASA Mars Trek provide great bird’s-eye views for scientists on Earth, but an astronaut standing on the surface needs immediate answers to stay alive: Is that ridge safe to cross? Will I make it back before dark? What is my radiation dose?

Mars Sentinel bridges the gap between robotic orbiters and human spacewalks. By packaging elevation, weather, and radiation data into an easy-to-read heads-up display, it gives future crews the autonomy they need to explore alien worlds safely without waiting on Earth-based mission control.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did We use?

  • Front-End: Modern vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and CSS3. Designed with high-contrast tactical palettes (cyan, amber, red) for clear visibility through helmet visors under harsh sun glare.
  • Mapping Engine: Leaflet.js customized with non-Earth planetary coordinates and Mars Trek tile streaming.
  • 3D Planetary Engine: Hand-coded in raw WebGL2 (globe.js)—rendering real MOLA vertex displacement at 60 FPS without the overhead of heavy third-party 3D libraries.
  • Data Processing & Testing: Python (GDAL, NumPy) to convert USGS elevation rasters into raw binary grids; Node.js test suite (tests/mars.test.js) to verify that the pathfinding math never breaches safety limits.
  • Hosting: Deployed on Vercel for fast edge delivery worldwide.
  • AI TOOLS: Antigravity- Claude, Gemini and GPT Models

5. How is Our project creative?

  • Combines 4 NASA Missions in One View: Unifies telemetry and observations from MRO (imagery and slope models), MGS (MOLA global elevation), MSL Curiosity (RAD radiation baseline: 0.64 mSv/day), and Mars 2020 Perseverance (live MEDA weather and sample sites).
  • "Shortest vs. Safest" Route Comparison: An interactive card shows the exact trade-off between routes. For example, taking the safer path only adds 5 minutes of walking time, but triples clearance from steep drop-offs from 50 meters to 131 meters.
  • Built-in Survival Guide: Integrates an interactive Survival Guide panel directly into the workflow, providing sector hazard ratings, ground rules, and consumable depletion warnings.

6. What factors did Our team consider?

  • Spacesuit Ergonomics: Pressurized EVA gloves eliminate fine-motor touch controls, and helmets restrict peripheral vision. We used large controls, high-contrast monospace text, and clear color warnings.
  • Operating Without GPS: With no satellite constellation on Mars, routes are anchored to visible HiRISE terrain landmarks so astronauts can visually cross-check their path.
  • Martian Diurnal Freezing Risk: Jezero Crater temperatures plummet to −79.3 °C at night, and daylight ends at 17:13 (late autumn). The system factors in remaining sunlight so crews are never caught outside after dark.
  • Zero-Trust Safety Principle: Any unmapped pixel or grid edge is mathematically treated as a hazard. In space exploration, assuming missing data is "safe" is how accidents happen.
